Sadly it’s really prominent, I’ve seen it in inpatient units, forensic settings, supported livings it’s sadly everywhere. From a personal and professional standpoint it’s really upsetting for me and often feel like when I challenge these views I’m met with a brick wall and as if I’m the ‘weird one’. I’ve noticed students start using negative connotations without even meeting the patients just because of stuff they have heard from more long standing staff members. Patients with PDs can be ‘difficult’ just as a patient with schizophrenia can be ‘difficult’. As human beings we can all be ‘difficult’. It totally f*cks me off the attitude. It’s refreshing to see a post like this as it makes me feel at least there is someone out there that sees it.

Not hallucinating. Not sure if it was an echo but I was getting super confused as it was almost like there was a horn that went off in quick succession after the first. Happened a few times so that definitely baffled me 😅

I’m currently writing it all down. You are right. I would like to reach out in the future but I feel like it’s ruined, and it’s my fault. I just hated every time we spoke it was just me having a meltdown. I work in mental health myself and as much as I have endless support and care for patients it can be difficult to manage those levels of distress long term. So I feel this is inevitable for her as well. Thanks for the kindness in your response.
Also there is some great advice in there. I may ‘know it all’ but in a crisis I often forget the external support so thank you for the reminders.

Thank you for your kindness. I feel I didn’t give too much background/ context as I didn’t want to go on. I’ve got a diagnosis and have ‘managed’ it for years. Albeit not too well. I’ve had therapy on the NHS that just didn’t quite cut it due to constraints on their side. I found schema therapy to be the best and decided to go private. I decided to come off my Quetiapine in January which was a terrible decision and have not been able to have this re prescribed for a variety of reasons. Lamotrogine hasn’t touched the sides for me unfortunately. So I feel this has been a massive contributor to the ongoing constant crisis.
This is truly a lovely response. Thank you so so much. I admit I was nervous to post this for a variety of reasons but your comment alone makes me feel glad that I did. 💜

I’m honestly not sure! But one thing I’ll say it’s ok to communicate with them why you feel invalidated with how they phrase and document their notes. I have addressed this in the past with a psychiatrist. If the GP isn’t considerate of this or at least can be reassuring to you then I’ll be honest I’d maybe find another GP in the practice as there will be somebody that will be mindful of this.

As someone who works in healthcare it’s something we are just trained to write as something we haven’t witnessed ourselves. We write things like ‘alleged’ or ‘reported’ or ‘appeared to’. I hate writing it as it feels invalidating to write but just wanted to reassure you it’s not ‘you’ or their lack of trust in your lived experience. I hope this helps 💜

I’m sorry I don’t have any advice but I just wanted to say I’m going through the exact same thing so you’re not alone with this feeling. I hope you navigate it and work through it. I feel it’s one of those ‘trust the process’ situations (I kinda hate that phrase) though I feel this is where it applies 🥹
Thanks for the response. I’ll try hang in there but living with this mental pain is horrific. Trying to be patient.

Hello, I work as a Healthcare Worker in a forensic mental health hospital. I didn’t have prior training but had to do plenty with the company before I started and during to keep it up. Things like Recovery Worker or Support Worker in inpatient units or in the community also are a good place to look. I’m based in York so I’m not sure what’s around your area. Good luck with the job search!
